Reviewer notes on manuscript NCOMMS-25-16381
The paper of Romero and co-workers provides an insight into the soil microbiome as indicator of function
across Europe. It is an actual topic that is important for the future of sustainable food systems. The work is
novel and impactful by looking at a large number of sites across Europe and by combining amplicon
sequencing data (16S rRNA gene & ITS sequences) with indicators of microbial abundance (such as
microbial biomass) and activity (enzymes). The large dataset on 500 soils across Europe is of interest for
the scientific community. The paper is overall well written and I enjoyed reading the work.
Having said this, I have some larger points of feedback, mainly focusing on the set-up of the study and the
claimed impact on soil multifunctionality and agriculture.
Multifunctionality is a central point of the paper. Overall “multifunctionality” would benefit from a better
definition at the start. What is multifunctionality within the context of your work, which main processes do
you target and how do the parameters link to that? It is important to stay close to your own work to avoid
speculating too much.
Regarding the conclusions and claims, I miss a section on the limitations and perspectives of this work. In
line with the more specific comments given below, it would be very useful to provide an overview of the
current limitations and challenges of this work. This would, in my opinion, better embed it within the current
research field, and it would better highlight the added value of this work without overinterpretation of the
work / the risk of speculation.
The figures are overall clear, and they provide good visual support for the written text. I can see that this
has been a lot of work and I appreciate the efforts. The supplementary figures further support the work and
they facilitate future research on the topic.
I have added my comments, linking to the points mentioned above under a major comments section. The
minor comments section contains mainly minor textual and structural suggestions.
Major comments
- Overall, the pooling of all sampled soils in three major categories seems rather rough, as you showed
earlier that there are quite big differences in microbial composition between different woodland soils:
Coniferous wood and broadleaved wood was always significantly different in fungal and bacterial richness
and Shannon diversity (Labouyrie 2023). In addition, it is known that you find major differences in microbial
communities of clay soils and sandy soils. This is not addressed in the paper, but it does need some
attention.
In addition, it is known that the pH has a strong effect on microbial communities. How does the relatively
low pH of e.g. pine forests affect the results?
The consequence of zooming out to these three major categories is that you obtain very general
microbiomes.
-The z-score needs to be better embedded/introduced. A range of functions is mentioned in the introduction,
but not all are represented in the z-score.
If I see it correctly, the non-weighted calculation of z-score is based for 50% on enzymatic OM decomposing
activity, and the rest on net primary productivity, microbial biomass and aggregation is used to draw the
conclusion that multifunctionality is driven by microbial factors. Individual graphs per cover type do not
support the claim that the z-score is driven by microbial factors (Supplementary figure 2), neither do the
SEM, and rather point at edaphic parameters to be driving the z-score
I miss the reasoning on why you think these three enzymes can define (half of) multifunctionality.
-The sampling time in spring makes it challenging to compare (mainly) the cropland to the grassland and
woodland sites. Please also discuss this in the paper.
-The paper stresses a lot on taxa as valuable multifunctionality indicators. The focus on three major areas
however has several limitations, which should be better discussed. At the end the need for conservation
strategies that preserve microbial-driven functions in diverse land uses are highlighted. However, by
focusing on three major land use types and using DNA-based taxonomy at higher taxonomic level this feels
like a bridge too far. It is very speculative.
The link to the z-score is also relevant here: The z-score cannot tell multifunctionality from grasslands and
forests apart, how useful is it then in practice?
-Is there a specific reason/motivation to not include AMF in the work? AMF were e.g. included in the work of
Labouyrie (2023), but not in this work. It is good to, at least, shortly mention the motivation for not
including this here.
-I could not find a link to the sequencing data (online archive). This needs to be included.
Minor comments

rephrase.
-Line 52-53: you focus on functions at different levels/magnitudes. It is useful to have a look at Creamer et

function, but water holding capacity is a smaller part of “water regulation and purification”.
